title: August and the Witness
premise: When insurance investigator Jonah Sandoval receives a confession letter for a fifteen-year-old drowning ruled accidental, he recognizes the handwriting as his own — copied from a file he memorized and burned. The letter's author is someone who studied him as closely as he studied the town, and they begin feeding him fragments of the night Harlan Voss died, each one implicating someone Jonah loves. As the trial of the wrongfully accused man approaches, Jonah must reconstruct his own buried memory of that night, discovering he was the sole witness and that his perfect memory was deliberately edited by grief. In the end, Jonah traps the killer — the town's beloved retired sheriff, who has been orchestrating the confession to force the truth into the open before dying of cancer — but must choose between exposing a dying man's justice or letting the innocent man hang.
about_author: Orsen Eriksen is the pen name of a former claims adjuster from the Pacific Northwest who spent a decade reading other people's disasters for a living. August and the Witness is their second novel, written in the margins of a life spent alphabetizing other people's losses.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Jonah Sandoval, POV. Three days after Harlan Voss's mother is buried, a confession letter arrives describing her son's drowning in detail only a witness could know. Jonah's photographic memory flags an impossibility: the handwriting mimics his own. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional curiosity, the first crack in fifteen years of filed-away certainty.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Jonah, POV. He pulls the original case file and finds pages subtly altered — dates shifted, a witness statement missing. His mentor, retired sheriff Dale Pruitt, warns him off with unusual urgency. Meanwhile, the letter's second installment arrives, naming a date Jonah has no memory of despite having been in town. Beat: the investigator becomes the investigated; unease curdles into obsession.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Jonah in the present, fragmented sensory flashes of a rainy August night fifteen years ago — a dock, a scream, hands. He interviews the drowned boy's sister, Maren, who reveals the accused man, Toby Ellery, confessed under pressure and recanted. Beat: grief surfaces through the cracks of a memory that refuses to play back whole.

chapters.title: A Man Who Files Everything
chapters.summary: Maren, POV. She watches Jonah work and realizes he isn't investigating the letter — he's investigating himself. She shares Harlan's letters home, which mention a fight the night he died involving someone 'with a badge.' Jonah's third letter arrives quoting one of those letters verbatim, though it was never in any file. Beat: the hunter realizes the trap is shaped exactly like him.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Jonah, POV. He reconstructs his own timeline and finds a two-week gap in August — erased not by trauma alone but by deliberate avoidance; he'd requested leave, left town, come back changed. Dale Pruitt's name keeps surfacing in the gap's edges. Beat: loyalty begins to rot as Jonah admits the person he trusts most may be the person he's afraid of.

chapters.title: The Confession Machine
chapters.summary: Toby Ellery, POV (a first for the novel). From county jail, Toby describes his interrogation by young Deputy Pruitt fifteen years ago — the pressure, the planted details, the recantation no one printed. A fourth letter reaches Toby directly, promising exoneration if he stays silent until trial. Beat: hope weaponized; the reader sees the killer is engineering the trial itself.

chapters.title: Everything I Remember Is a Lie
chapters.summary: Jonah, POV. Under hypnosis-adjacent self-interrogation using his own filing techniques, Jonah recovers the full night: he saw Dale Pruitt strike Harlan on the dock during a drunken confrontation, and Dale — his father's best friend — helped him bury the memory out of 'mercy.' Beat: devastating midpoint reversal; the witness was always himself.

chapters.title: Trial by Letter
chapters.summary: Maren and Jonah, alternating. With the trial ten days out, the letters escalate, now threatening to expose Jonah's suppressed testimony and destroy both cases. They trace the postmarks to the hospice wing where Dale is being treated for terminal cancer. Confronting him yields only a smile: 'You finally read the whole file.' Beat: rising panic — justice is on a deadline.

chapters.title: The Last Filing Error
chapters.summary: Jonah, POV. Dale, dying, confesses everything in a recorded conversation he assumes Jonah will destroy — but Jonah springs his trap: he'd already given copies to the prosecutor and Maren, forcing Dale to testify before he dies and free Toby. Dale's motive: he wanted the truth dragged out by the one person whose memory couldn't lie forever. Beat: climax — justice outside the law, achieved by turning the law's own machinery.

chapters.title: Alphabetized at Last
chapters.summary: Jonah, POV, epilogue after Dale's death. Toby walks free; Maren and Jonah sort Harlan's belongings together, and Jonah files the confession letter under 'V' — the last entry in his private archive of the town's secrets. He burns his old system and starts a blank notebook. Beat: bittersweet resolution — truth cost him his cleanest comfort, memory, and bought something harder: a future unfiled.
